prompt.context: Your client builds elevators for both residential and commercial buildings. The CEO is worried because in the last couple of months they have been losing money even though total sales have remained almost at the same level.
prompt.question: What is wrong and how can it be rectified?

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's market position?
clarifying_info.a: The client is the largest residential elevator manufacturer in the U.S. It also recently grew to become the second largest commercial elevator manufacturer.

clarifying_info.q: Has the product mix changed recently?
clarifying_info.a: Originally, they sold mainly to residential buildings. Due to the downturn, residential building sales have dropped. On the other hand, they have sold more elevators to commercial buildings.

exhibits.title: Cost structure and sales distribution
exhibits.shows: A table showing costs as a percentage of sales for residential vs. commercial elevators (Material, Manufacture, Labor, Plant, Sales commissions), and the current sales mix split between Residential and Commercial.

framework: Define profitability issue: revenues vs. costs — total sales flat but losses growing suggests cost or mix problem
Analyze revenue mix: has the split between residential and commercial shifted?
Analyze cost structure by segment: compare margin for residential vs. commercial
Identify root cause of margin difference: higher material and manufacturing costs in commercial
Quantify impact: calculate blended margin given current sales mix
Recommend fixes: reduce commercial costs (supplier negotiation, labor, equipment investment) and/or reprice

questions.prompt: After reviewing Exhibit 1, what is the margin for residential and commercial elevators, and what is causing the overall loss?
questions.guidance: Residential margin: 100% - (20+20+30+19+7)% = 100% - 96% = 4% margin. Commercial margin: 100% - (24+29+30+19+7)% = 100% - 109% = -9% margin. Commercial sales account for 55% of total sales, and at -9% margin they are dragging down overall profitability. Commercial elevators have higher material costs (24% vs 20%, i.e., 20% higher) and higher manufacturing costs (29% vs 20%, i.e., 45% higher) compared to residential.

math.setup: Sum all cost line items for each segment and subtract from 100% to get margin.
steps: Commercial accounts for 55% of sales, so losses from commercial more than offset residential gains
math.answer: Residential margin = 4%; Commercial margin = -9%; the shift in mix toward commercial (55% of sales) is causing overall losses.

questions.prompt: How would you get profits from commercial elevators and what would the margin goal be?
questions.guidance: The commercial elevator margin should be raised to at least 4% (matching residential) if not higher. To achieve this, the client should reduce material and manufacturing costs — the two areas where commercial is significantly more expensive. Specific levers: (1) negotiate with suppliers to reduce material costs; (2) reduce labor or improve labor productivity; (3) invest in more efficient or different manufacturing equipment to lower manufacture costs. Pricing increases are also an option but depend on market competitiveness.

questions.prompt: A new customer arrives with a draft of a new commercial skyscraper and wants your services at current prices. Would you advise your client to sell to them?
questions.guidance: The answer is 'it depends.' At current prices, each commercial elevator sold generates a -9% loss, so the deal loses money outright. However, selling into a high-profile skyscraper project may serve as a marketing strategy: it can boost brand recognition and enable the client to win future contracts at higher (profitable) prices. The client should only accept if: (a) they can frame it as a deliberate brand investment and (b) they have a credible plan to leverage that recognition to renegotiate or raise prices on future commercial deals.

recommendation: The client is losing money because the shift in sales mix toward commercial elevators (now 55% of sales) has introduced a -9% margin segment that outweighs the 4% margin from residential

The client should invest in reducing commercial elevator material and manufacturing costs — ideally closing the gap to match residential margins — through supplier renegotiation, labor efficiency, and equipment investment
risks: If cost reduction efforts fail or take time, losses will continue to mount as commercial volume stays high
Accepting the skyscraper deal at current prices locks in a loss unless it translates into concrete future pricing power
next_steps: Conduct detailed cost analysis to identify specific cost-reduction opportunities in commercial manufacturing
Negotiate with key suppliers on material costs
Evaluate capital investment options (equipment) that reduce per-unit manufacture cost
Develop a commercial pricing strategy that reflects true cost-to-serve once margin targets are achievable
If pursuing the skyscraper deal, define explicit marketing KPIs and a timeline for translating brand exposure into improved pricing
